title: Gleaning in the Field of Boaz
summary: Ruth goes out to glean grain behind the harvesters and happens to come to the field of Boaz, a wealthy relative of Elimelech. Boaz, who has heard of her loyalty to Naomi, protects her, feeds her, and quietly tells his workers to leave extra grain for her. She brings home an ephah of barley, and Naomi, learning whose field it was, blesses the LORD and reveals that Boaz is one of their kinsman-redeemers.
story: Chapter 1 ended with two widows arriving in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest, Naomi calling herself empty. Chapter 2 begins to fill that emptiness. Ruth, the Moabite outsider, takes the initiative to provide for them both, and the story introduces Boaz, whose name the narrator gives in the first verse before Ruth or Naomi knows it. The chapter moves from Ruth's hope of finding favor to her finding it, and ends with Naomi's first word of blessing in the book. Naomi, who had said the LORD was against her, now says he has not withdrawn his kindness from the living or the dead. The chapter sets up the problem the rest of the book will solve: Boaz is a redeemer, but will he act as one?
historical:
The barley harvest in Judah came in the spring, around April, and the wheat harvest followed in late spring and early summer; the chapter covers both (2:23), a period of perhaps seven weeks. This is the season between Passover and the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot, also called Pentecost), and Jewish tradition reads Ruth at Shavuot for that reason.

Israel's law provided for the poor, the foreigner, the widow, and the fatherless through the right to glean. Leviticus 19:9-10 and 23:22 told landowners not to reap to the very edges of their fields or gather what fell during the harvest, and Deuteronomy 24:19-22 told them to leave forgotten sheaves for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. Ruth was all three kinds of vulnerable person the law named, foreign, widowed, and without a father nearby. Not every landowner honored these laws, and a foreign woman gleaning alone could be mistreated, which is why Boaz's protection matters.
cultural:
The harvest was communal work. Men cut the standing grain with sickles, and women followed to bind it into sheaves, with gleaners coming behind to pick up what was left. Boaz's greeting to his workers, “The LORD be with you” (2:4), and their reply show a household in which faith shaped ordinary speech. The foreman and the young men and women were hired laborers; Boaz is described as a man of standing and substance, the Hebrew gibbor chayil, a phrase that can mean a mighty warrior but here means a man of wealth, influence, and worth.

Boaz's generosity goes well beyond the law's requirement. He invites Ruth to stay with his workers, to drink from their water jars, and to eat with them, and he tells his young men to pull grain out of the bundles for her. Her ephah of barley was a large amount for one day's gleaning; estimates of an ephah vary, but it was enough to feed two women for some weeks. The kinsman-redeemer (go'el) was a close relative responsible for helping a family in trouble: buying back land that had been sold (Leviticus 25:25), redeeming a relative sold into slavery (Leviticus 25:47-49), and avenging a murdered relative. Naomi's recognition that Boaz is a go'el opens the door to the rest of the story.
literary: The chapter is built around a series of conversations: Ruth and Naomi (2:2), Boaz and his foreman (2:5-7), Boaz and Ruth (2:8-14), and Ruth and Naomi again (2:19-22). The narrator's comment that Ruth happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz (2:3) uses a phrase that literally means her chance chanced upon it, a deliberately understated way of pointing to providence. Boaz's arrival is introduced with a Hebrew word often translated behold, and the timing is striking. The key word hesed returns in 2:20, where Naomi blesses the LORD for his kindness. Boaz's blessing on Ruth, that she has taken refuge under the LORD's wings (2:12), uses the image of a bird sheltering its young. In chapter 3 Ruth will ask Boaz to spread his wing, the corner of his garment, over her, which invites Boaz to become the answer to his own prayer.

outline.t: Boaz introduced, and Ruth goes out to glean
Boaz arrives and asks about the young woman
The meal and the extra grain
Naomi learns of Boaz, the kinsman-redeemer

doctrines.note: Ruth happens to come to the field of Boaz. The narrator's understatement invites the reader to see God's hand in what looks like chance, without any miracle. God guides ordinary events for his purposes.

The gleaning laws of Leviticus and Deuteronomy made room for the poor and the foreigner in Israel's harvest. Boaz keeps the law and goes beyond it, showing that its purpose was generosity, not minimum compliance.
Boaz blesses Ruth as one who has taken refuge under the wings of the LORD. The image describes a foreigner finding shelter in Israel's God, which the prophets and New Testament extend to all nations.

words.note: Ga'al, to redeem, and the participle go'el, kinsman-redeemer. In 2:20 Naomi says Boaz is one of their redeemers. The go'el was a near relative with the right and duty to buy back land, free a relative from slavery, or avenge a death. The word is also used of God as Israel's redeemer (Exodus 6:6; Isaiah 43:1), and it becomes the book's central idea.

Hesed, loyal love or kindness. In 2:20 Naomi blesses the LORD, who has not withdrawn his hesed from the living or the dead. The grammar could refer to Boaz or to the LORD, and interpreters differ, but the point is similar either way: God's faithfulness is reaching Naomi through Boaz's generosity.

Kanaph, wing, and also the corner or edge of a garment. Boaz speaks of the LORD's wings under which Ruth has taken refuge (2:12). The same word returns in 3:9 when Ruth asks Boaz to spread the corner of his garment over her. The echo is deliberate, and it links divine protection with human action.

Miqreh, chance or happening, used in 2:3 in the phrase her chance chanced upon the field of Boaz. The narrator uses the language of chance with a wink, since the reader knows that in this book nothing is really accidental. It is one of the Old Testament's most elegant descriptions of providence.

christ: The central idea introduced here, the kinsman-redeemer, is used by the New Testament to describe what Christ does. The Old Testament speaks of God as Israel's redeemer, buying back his people from slavery (Exodus 6:6), and the New Testament says Christ redeemed us at the cost of his own blood (1 Peter 1:18-19; Galatians 4:4-5). Hebrews stresses that Christ became our kinsman by sharing flesh and blood (Hebrews 2:14-17), which the Old Testament go'el required. Boaz's welcome of a foreign woman, his protection and provision beyond what the law demanded, and his blessing her for taking refuge under God's wings also echo in the gospel, where Jesus longs to gather Jerusalem's children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings (Matthew 23:37). These are patterns that the New Testament fills out, not hidden predictions.
questions: Ruth happened to come to Boaz's field. Looking back, where can you see God's hand in events that seemed like chance at the time?
Boaz kept the gleaning law and went beyond it. What would generosity beyond the minimum look like in your work, business, or community?
Naomi moved from bitterness to blessing when she saw God's kindness through Boaz. How can others be the means through which God's kindness reaches someone who is grieving?
